lines.english: The great mausoleum in Talas,
Beside the great mausoleum,
For Manas, who had gone to the other world,
She said, "Amen," and recited a blessing,
The sura called "Tabbat"
She recited astonishingly fast.
When she looked over this way:
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz stretched across the plain,
lines.note: The phrase "oy tartyp" can describe spreading or moving out over low, open ground; "stretched across the plain" is a contextual reading.

lines.english: They were encamped there,
Kumis by day, girls by night—
Such was the time they were having.
Wearing sable caps side by side,
lines.note: "Koshtop" literally conveys pairing or accompanying; its precise force with the caps is uncertain.

lines.english: They were swaying to and fro,
The Kyrgyz lamented together,
And lived in delight.
At that time the Kyrgyz people
Took whole otter skins
And split them lengthwise,
They were a tree planted in Talas,
lines.note: "Bak" can mean a tree, garden, or good fortune; the line appears to use it as an image of the flourishing people.

lines.english: And this was their time of strutting about.
At that time, among the Kyrgyz,
Even a poor man drove a thousand sheep,
And his old wife chewed fat-tail.
Of the seething, thriving Kyrgyz,
Which ailment could I tell?
With kelengker hair pendants and broad rumps,
lines.note: "Kelengker" is retained because the particular type or material of this traditional hair ornament is uncertain.

lines.english: The Kyrgyz daughters-in-law were beautiful,
In red dresses, with crescent-slender waists,
The Kyrgyz girls were beautiful,
In black robes and white kalpaks,
The Kyrgyz people were beautiful.
They had more rice than black grain,
lines.note: "Black grain" translates the source literally; the specific grain meant is uncertain.

lines.english: More silver than tin,
More foxes than gray hares,
Much wealth piled at their thresholds,
And what they wore was fox and sable.
Having wandered as an orphan and grown to manhood,
Having been reunited with his homeland,
lines.note: The source literally says that his head was joined to the land or home region; this is read idiomatically as reunion with his homeland.

lines.english: Semetey became leader of the people.
Aichurok did not know this,
And stood amazed at what she saw.
What the warriors wore
Were black caps of blue-gray lynx,
And all the warriors
Were uniformly alike, dark blue.
Beneath them they had thoroughbred mounts,
When six or seven of them set out,
They had the strength to face Chynkojo.
lines.note: The compact form "Chynkojoluk" is read as strength sufficient for or directed against Chynkojo; the exact grammatical relation is uncertain.

lines.english: The mounts ridden by them all
Were black-bay warhorses,
lines.note: "Kazanat" denotes a fine or heroic riding horse; "black-bay" reflects the color wording in the source.

lines.english: With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs.
The lands of Jylgynduu, Keng-Kol, and Talas
She saw and rejoiced,
And now Aichurok lived in delight.
The great mausoleum in Talas—
beside the great mausoleum,
for Manas, who had gone to the other world,
she said, "Amen," and recited a blessing,
and the sura called "Tabbat"
she recited with astonishing speed.
lines.note: The Kyrgyz phrasing can also suggest that she recited quickly as though astonished.

lines.english: When she looked over this way:
the Argyn and Kyrgyz had spread across the valley
lines.note: The compact phrase "ой тартып" is read as spreading or extending over the low ground.

lines.english: and were encamped there,
kumis by day and girls by night—
such was the time they were having.
Wearing sable caps in pairs,
lines.note: The wording may instead mean wearing matching sable caps.

lines.english: they were swaying to and fro,
the Kyrgyz singing laments together
and enjoying themselves.
At that time the Kyrgyz people
took whole otter pelts
and slit them lengthwise.
It was fortune planted in Talas,
lines.note: The image is literally of "bak"—fortune, or possibly a garden/tree—planted in Talas.

lines.english: a time when they strutted proudly.
At that time, among the Kyrgyz,
even a poor man drove a thousand sheep,
and his old wife chewed fat tail.
Of the Kyrgyz, seething with abundance,
which trouble shall I tell?
lines.note: The question is ironic in this catalogue of prosperity and beauty.

lines.english: With kelengker braid ornaments and broad rumps,
lines.note: "Kelengker" is retained because the precise material or type of the women's braid ornament is uncertain.

lines.english: the Kyrgyz daughters-in-law were beautiful;
in red dresses, with crescent-like waists,
the Kyrgyz maidens were beautiful;
in black robes and white kalpaks,
the Kyrgyz people were beautiful.
There was more rice than dark grain,
lines.note: "Dark grain" translates an unspecific grain category literally.

lines.english: more silver than tin,
more foxes than gray hares,
much wealth piled at their thresholds;
what they wore was fox and sable.
Having wandered as an orphan and come of age,
having rejoined his people,
lines.note: The literal idiom is "his head joined the community/land."

lines.english: Semetey had become the people's leader.
Aichurok did not know this;
she stood amazed at what she saw.
The young men wore
dark caps of blue-gray lynx;
lines.note: Color terms and their attachment are compressed: this may mean black caps made from blue-gray lynx.

lines.english: all the young men
were alike, uniformly blue-black.
lines.note: The line may refer to their dress or appearance rather than complexion.

lines.english: They had thoroughbred steeds beneath them;
when six or seven rode forth,
they had the strength of Chynkojo.
lines.note: The heroic comparison's exact force may be that the group collectively possessed Chynkojo-like strength.

lines.english: All of them rode
black bayir warhorses,
lines.note: "Bayir" is retained as an uncertain horse type or epithet; "kazanat" denotes a prized riding or war horse.

lines.english: with sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs.
lines.note: A literal heroic formula describing the horses' endurance and strength; "forelegs" is inferred from the anatomical context, though the word literally means arms.

lines.english: The lands of Jylgynduu, Keng-Kol, and Talas—
seeing those lands, she rejoiced,
and now Aichurok was filled with delight.
The great mausoleum in Talas,
Beside the great mausoleum,
For Manas, who had gone to the other world,
She offered a prayer, saying, ‘Amen,’
The sura called ‘Tabbat,’
She recited swiftly, as though astonished.
When she looked this way:
Argyns and Kyrgyz were deep in thought,
It was the time when they were encamped,
Kumis by day, girls by night,
It was a time of such things.
Wearing marten caps in matching pairs,
It was a time when they swayed about,
The Kyrgyz, joining in lament,
It was a time when they lived in delight.
At that time the Kyrgyz people
Had whole sable skins
Slit open and taken off,
A garden they had planted in Talas,
It was flourishing luxuriantly.
At that time among the Kyrgyz,
Even a poor man drove a thousand sheep,
An old woman chewed fat tail,
Of the Kyrgyz, seething with abundance,
Which of their troubles could I tell?
With kelengker headgear and broad hips,
lines.note: Uncertain: kelengker appears to name a style of women's headdress.

lines.english: The Kyrgyz daughters-in-law were beautiful,
In red dresses, with waists like the moon,
The Kyrgyz daughters were beautiful,
In black coats and white felt hats,
The Kyrgyz people were beautiful,
There was much rice from black grain,
There was much silver from their tin,
There were more foxes than white hares,
They had much wealth piled by the threshold,
They wore fox and ermine.
The orphan had grown to maturity,
And had joined his head to the people,
Semetey had become the leader of the people.
Aichurok did not know this,
She stood amazed at this sight,
What their heroes wore
Were black caps of blue lynx fur,
All their heroes
Were alike, dark blue throughout.
They had swift steeds beneath them,
When six or seven came together,
They had the strength of Chynkozhol.
lines.note: Uncertain: Chynkozhol is likely a proper name or a fixed epic epithet.

lines.english: What they all rode
Were black bay battle-horses,
With sieve-like lungs and bronze arms.
lines.note: The line uses compressed heroic imagery; the precise force of ‘sieve-like lungs’ is uncertain.

lines.english: Willow-rich Ken-Kol and Talas,
Seeing those lands, she rejoiced,
And now Aichurok was content.
The great mausoleum in Talas,
Beside that great mausoleum,
For Manas, who had gone to the other world,
She recited a blessing, saying “Amen,”
The surah called “Tappat”
lines.note: The surah’s name is retained as given in the source.

lines.english: She recited astonishingly fast.
When she looked this way:
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz, making for the lowlands,
lines.note: “Ой тартып” is read as moving toward low ground; the phrase is uncertain.

lines.english: Were encamped there at that time,
Kumys by day, girls by night—
That was how things were then.
Wearing marten-fur caps in pairs,
lines.note: The force of “коштоп” is uncertain: it may describe paired wearers rather than doubled caps.

lines.english: They were swaying at that time,
The Kyrgyz, joining one another,
Were living in delight at that time.
At that time the Kyrgyz people
Whole beaver pelts
Had slit open,
It was good fortune planted in Talas,
lines.note: “Бак” can mean either good fortune or a garden; “planted” preserves the imagery of the source.

lines.english: It was a time of exuberant flourishing.
lines.note: The expressive “талталаңдап” suggests expansive, carefree movement; its precise imagery here is uncertain.

lines.english: At that time, among the Kyrgyz,
Even a poor man drove a thousand sheep,
Even an old woman chewed sheep-tail fat.
Of the Kyrgyz, teeming with life,
Which sorrow shall I tell?
With kelengker braid ornaments and broad haunches,
lines.note: “Келеңкер” appears to specify a kind of braid ornament; its exact material or form is uncertain.

lines.english: The Kyrgyz daughters-in-law were beautiful,
In red dresses, with moonlike waists,
lines.note: The unusual comparison “айча бел” is preserved literally.

lines.english: The Kyrgyz girls were beautiful,
In black coats and white kalpaks,
The Kyrgyz people were beautiful,
There was more rice than dark grain,
lines.note: The precise crop meant by “кара эгин” is uncertain; “dark grain” retains its literal sense.

lines.english: More silver than tin,
More foxes than gray hares,
Much wealth piled at their thresholds,
They wore fox fur and sable.
Having grown to maturity as an orphan,
Having joined the ranks of his people,
Semetey had become the people’s leader.
Aichurok did not know this,
And was astonished at this state of affairs.
What their men wore
Was blue-gray lynx fur and black fur caps,
lines.note: The compressed phrase may instead describe black caps made of blue-gray lynx fur.

lines.english: Their men, every one,
Were uniformly alike, dark blue.
lines.note: “Кара көк” literally denotes a dark blue shade, but may carry a figurative description of the men here.

lines.english: They had swift steeds beneath them,
When six or seven went together,
They had the strength of Chynkozho.
lines.note: “Чынкожолук” is read as a comparison with the person Chynkozho.

lines.english: What all of them rode
Were kara-baiyr battle steeds,
lines.note: “Кара байыр” is retained as a horse designation; its exact breed or descriptive force is uncertain.

lines.english: With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs.
Of Zhylgynduu, Keng-Kol, and Talas,
lines.note: “Жылгындуу” is read as a place name, though it could mean “covered with tamarisk.”

lines.english: Seeing the land, she rejoiced,
And now Aichurok was delighting in it.
